title: Episode 241: Harriet Tubman: Moses of Her People, the Underground Railroad, and the Combahee River Raid
description:
The fearless life of Harriet Tubman: escaping Maryland slavery with a cracked skull, guiding seventy enslaved souls to freedom on the Underground Railroad without losing a single passenger, and leading the Combahee River military raid in the Civil War.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome back to Most Fascinating Stories. Today, our chronicle of the Top 50 Famous Non-President Americans follows the most audacious, fearless, and legendary conductor of the Underground Railroad: Harriet Tubman.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: ARAMINTA ROSS AND THE BUCKTOWN DRY GOODS STORE
In the early 1820s, in the tidal marshlands of Dorchester County, Maryland, a girl named Araminta 'Minty' Ross was born into chattel slavery to Ben and Rit Green Ross. From early childhood, Minty was hired out to cruel masters: checking muskrat traps in freezing swamp water, caring for infants with a whip hanging over her cradle, and laboring in the timber forests alongside her father, acquiring exceptional physical endurance, woodsman skills, and an intimate knowledge of forest navigation. In 1835, when she was barely thirteen years old, Minty accompanied a cook to the village dry goods store at Bucktown Crossroads. An enraged overseer cornered a young enslaved boy who had left the fields without permission, raising a heavy, two-pound iron weight from the store counter to throw at the boy. Minty stepped into the doorway, positioning her own small body to shield the runaway. The heavy iron weight struck her squarely in the forehead, crushing her skull. She hovered between life and death for months on a straw pallet. The injury left her with lifelong narcoleptic seizures, splitting headaches, and sudden sleeping spells, but also profound, vivid spiritual visions and prophetic dreams that she regarded as direct divine communiqués from God Almighty.  The tidal marshes of Dorchester County were rich in loblolly pine and white oak, where young Minty learned to read animal tracks, predict weather changes, and move silently through dense underbrush without snapping a twig.  The overseer who struck Harriet with the iron weight at Bucktown was attempting to stop another slave who had fled to the store without an official written pass.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE FLIGHT TO FREEDOM: 1849
In 1844, Minty married a free Black man named John Tubman and took her mother's name, becoming Harriet Tubman. In the autumn of 1849, upon the death of her master Edward Brodess, rumors spread that Harriet and her brothers were about to be sold away to the cotton plantations of the Deep South, tearing the family apart forever. John Tubman refused to leave Maryland, threatening to betray her to the overseers if she attempted to run away. Harriet resolved to follow her conscience alone: 'There was one of two things I had a right to, liberty or death; if I could not have one, I would have the other.' Guided by Quaker abolitionists and free Black boatmen through the Underground Railroad, Harriet traveled ninety miles through Maryland and Delaware, navigating at night by following the North Star—the drinking gourd—wading through freezing creeks to mask her scent from bloodhounds. Crossing the Pennsylvania state border, she looked down at her hands to see if she was the same person: 'When I found I had crossed that line, I looked at my hands to see if I was the same person. There was such a glory over everything; the sun came like gold through the trees, and over the fields, and I felt like I was in Heaven.' But she immediately felt lonely: 'I was free, and they should be free too.'  When Harriet arrived in Philadelphia, she was welcomed by William Still, the heroic Black secretary of the Pennsylvania Anti-Slavery Society, who recorded the testimonies of escaping runaways in a secret ledger.  In Philadelphia, Harriet worked as a domestic cook in hotels and clubhouses, saving every penny of her wages to finance her rescue expeditions back to Maryland.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: MOSES OF HER PEOPLE: THE UNDERGROUND RAILROAD
Over the next ten years, Harriet Tubman performed deeds of courage that surpassed ancient mythology. Rather than enjoying her personal freedom in Philadelphia, she made nineteen perilous return journeys into the heart of slave territory on the Eastern Shore of Maryland, rescuing approximately seventy family members, friends, and strangers, and providing navigational instructions to fifty more. Known throughout the South simply as 'Moses', she operated with military precision: she scheduled escapes for Saturday nights because newspapers containing runaway rewards could not be published until Monday morning. She disguised herself as an elderly hunched woman or an eccentric field hand carrying two live chickens by their legs, releasing them to chase them in comical confusion whenever slave catchers approached. She carried paregoric to quiet crying babies, and carried a loaded revolver tucked into her apron skirt. If an exhausted, terrified runaway faltered and wanted to turn back—which would expose the secret routes, hiding places, and station masters of the Underground Railroad to southern torturers—Tubman pointed the pistol at their chest and whispered with chilling resolve: 'Move on or die; a dead man tells no tales.' In ten years of operations, she never had to pull the trigger, famously boasting: 'I never ran my train off the track, and I never lost a passenger.'  Tubman's spiritual faith was intense and direct: she believed that the sudden sleeping spells caused by her head injury were divine trances during which God revealed safe river crossings and warned her of slave catchers.  On one rescue mission, Harriet encountered her former master in a Maryland town; she immediately lowered her straw hat and pulled the strings of her live chickens, causing them to flap wildly and diverting his attention.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: JOHN BROWN, 'GENERAL TUBMAN', AND THE GATHERING STORM
Following the passage of the draconian federal Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, which permitted southern slave catchers to kidnap Black citizens from northern streets, Tubman redirected her escape routes hundreds of miles further north into St. Catharines, Ontario, Canada, placing her passengers under the protection of the British Crown. In 1858, in Boston, Tubman met the fiery radical abolitionist John Brown. Brown was so awed by Tubman's strategic brilliance, topographical genius, and unyielding courage that he referred to her as 'General Tubman', declaring her 'the most of a man of any person I ever saw'. Tubman helped Brown recruit volunteers and plan his daring assault on the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, intended to spark a massive slave liberation uprising throughout the Appalachian mountains. Only severe illness prevented Tubman from participating in the ill-fated raid in October 1859. When Brown was hanged by Virginia authorities, Tubman mourned him as an immortal martyr of human freedom.  John Brown had sought Tubman's advice on the geography of the Blue Ridge Mountains, believing that her knowledge of escape routes was essential to establishing guerrilla redoubts in the Virginia wilderness.  John Brown had designated Tubman to be one of the top commanders in his provisional revolutionary army, giving her the official title of 'General' in his military correspondence.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: UNION SCOUT, SPY, AND NURSE: THE CIVIL WAR
When the Civil War erupted, Tubman recognized that the conflict offered the supreme opportunity to eradicate slavery forever. In 1862, Massachusetts Governor John Andrew dispatched Tubman to the Union-occupied Sea Islands of South Carolina, where thousands of enslaved refugees—contrabands of war—had gathered behind Union lines. Tubman worked as a nurse at Beaufort, brewing herbal remedies from roots and water lilies to cure Union soldiers suffering from dysentery and smallpox, without contracting the disease herself. Recognizing her unmatched knowledge of southern terrain and coastal waterways, Major General David Hunter recruited Tubman to establish a covert espionage network behind Confederate lines. Operating alongside former enslaved boatmen, fishermen, and scouts, Tubman mapped Confederate river fortifications, torpedo positions, and troop movements throughout the South Carolina lowcountry, reporting directly to Union headquarters.  In Beaufort, South Carolina, Tubman ran a laundry and bakery to support herself, refusing to accept pay from Union relief organizations so that resources could be directed to impoverished freedwomen and children.  During the Combahee River expedition, Tubman stood on the hurricane deck of the flagship alongside Colonel Montgomery, directing the pilots through Confederate river mines with absolute confidence.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE COMBAHEE RIVER RAID: JUNE 2, 1863
On the dark, moonless night of June 2, 1863, Harriet Tubman made military history as the first woman in United States history to plan and lead an armed military assault. In command of three federal gunboats—the John Adams, Sentinel, and Harriet A. Weed—carrying one hundred and fifty Black soldiers of the 2nd South Carolina Volunteer Infantry under Colonel James Montgomery, Tubman guided the vessels past underwater Confederate mines up the winding, crocodile-infested waters of the Combahee River. As federal troops landed at plantations, setting fire to Confederate cotton warehouses, rice mills, and bridges, steam whistles sounded from the gunboats. Thousands of enslaved people dropped their hoes and rushed to the riverbanks carrying babies, pots, and chickens, leaping into the shallows to reach the Union rescue boats. Confederate cavalry and artillery rushed to the scene, but were driven back by federal gunboat cannons. Over seven hundred and fifty enslaved human beings were liberated in a single night without the loss of a single Union soldier, many of the freed men enlisting immediately into the Union Army. Tubman later recalled the scene: 'I never saw such a sight; we laughed and laughed and laughed!'  The Combahee River raid was celebrated in national newspapers, with the Boston Commonwealth declaring that 'General Tubman has performed deeds of valor that surpass any female leader in military history.'  The Combahee River raid destroyed millions of dollars of Confederate property, including four rice mills, six cotton mansions, and thousands of barrels of rice intended for Lee's army in Virginia.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE AUBURN HEARTH AND THE ETERNAL LEGACY OF MOSES
Following the Union victory, Tubman settled in Auburn, New York, on land purchased from her friend, Secretary of State William H. Seward. For thirty years, the federal government shamefully denied her an official veteran's pension for her military scout and espionage services, granting her only a meager widow's pension of twenty dollars a month after the death of her second husband, Civil War veteran Nelson Davis. Despite living in near-poverty, Tubman threw open her home to orphaned children, elderly freedpeople, and the homeless, eventually establishing the Harriet Tubman Home for Aged and Indigent Negroes. In her final years, she became a fiery champion of women's suffrage, appearing alongside Susan B. Anthony at conventions across the Northeast. When she died on March 10, 1913, at approximately ninety-three years of age, she was buried with full military honors at Fort Hill Cemetery in Auburn, saluted by a military firing squad. Harriet Tubman remains an unshakeable monument of American heroism: the enslaved girl with a broken skull who became the Moses of her people, leading hundreds out of the valley of the shadow of death into the promised land of freedom.  Tubman's house in Auburn became a sanctuary for the helpless, where she cultivated an apple orchard, kept a vegetable garden, and tended pigs to feed elderly freedpeople who had nowhere else to turn in their final years.  In 2016, the United States Department of the Treasury announced that Harriet Tubman would be featured on the face of the twenty-dollar bill, honoring her as one of the greatest freedom fighters in American history.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. Next week, our Top 50 Non-President Americans series continues with Episode 242: Thomas Paine—Common Sense, The American Crisis, and the Firebrand of the American Revolution. Until then, stay curious.
